title: Induction heads and their phase change
description: Heads learn to continue patterns by copying tokens following earlier matches.

claims.heading: Induction heads copy continuations by combining with earlier heads attending to previous tokens
Induction heads emerge abruptly with early in-context learning gains and a loss bump
Do induction heads explain most loss improvement across token positions in large transformers?
Induction behaviour recurs across model families, sizes, training runs and modalities
Training data and setup affect induction heads and how long in-context learning lasts
Other mechanisms can carry most few-shot task learning
Induction heads can form through several ordered stages

related_findings.title: Induction beyond single-token matching
related_findings.summary: Small transformers learn induction over longer histories and copying delays selected by context. The depth and head capacity required depend on the task and architectural assumptions.

examples.headline: Multi-token induction needs more layers or first-layer heads when earlier attention uses positions alone.
Three-layer attention learns copying delays selected by context, while tested two-layer configurations fail.
Sufficient heads and dimensions let two-layer attention approximate induction over multi-token contexts.

related_findings.title: Induction spreads across changing sets of heads
related_findings.summary: Copying can survive removal of individual induction heads or identified head sets. Redundancy grows with scale, while its distribution varies across architectures.

examples.headline: Induction breaks after fewer head ablations in Qwen2.5 (grouped-query attention) than Pythia (multi-head attention).
Late Pythia checkpoints retain copying after any single-head ablation, with greater redundancy at scale.
Removing identified induction heads barely affects copying in a routed transformer; removing routing destroys it.

related_findings.title: Copying beyond standard attention
related_findings.summary: State-space and hybrid models can solve synthetic induction tasks, which test copying after repeats, and associative recall, which tests retrieving associated items. Performance and generalisation to different sequence lengths vary substantially, and task success alone does not identify an induction circuit.

examples.headline: H3 matches Attention on the synthetic induction task, without identifying learned circuits.
Geometric state-space model keeps induction accuracy high across lengths where Selective state-space model performance declines.
ReBased recalls multiple associated items more accurately than Based, but attention locates retrieval positions more precisely.

related_findings.title: Label copying helps classification and causes errors
related_findings.summary: Heads that attend to demonstration labels retrieve those labels and can supply useful task vectors, representations of the task. The same behaviour can follow incorrect labels or place too much weight on the most recent demonstration.

examples.headline: With permuted labels, disabling GPT-J heads matching same-class prefixes brings correct- and incorrect-label accuracies closer.
Injecting summed induction-head outputs as task vectors sharply improves Llama2-70B zero-shot classification.
Correct demonstrations can lower vision-language model accuracy as predictions shift toward the latest demonstration's label.

related_findings.title: Signals around circuit formation
related_findings.summary: Circuit formation shows up in measurements of loss-landscape shape, sensitivity to perturbations and spectral structure. Some signals precede changes in induction scores, while others accompany behaviour without predicting which head will emerge.

examples.headline: Measured sensitivities to induction attention patterns rise slowly, then accelerate during training.
RoPE spectral changes accompany previous-token behaviour but do not predict head identity beforehand.
Participation ratio, a measure of effective dimensionality, rises before induction scores.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Induction heads specialise and share functions
related_findings.summary: Induction heads differ in prefix-length preferences and contextual selectivity. A single head can support many token-specific induction features alongside unrelated functions.

examples.headline: GPT-2 Small induction heads differ in whether they need long prefixes for strong matching.
Llama2-7b induction heads attend to context-licensed repeats in disjunctions but not list controls.
One induction head supports suffix-specific induction features and non-induction code-completion features.

related_findings.title: Induction within a broader developmental sequence
related_findings.summary: Induction can precede function-vector heads and attention sinks, with some heads changing roles during training. The apparent sharpness of later abilities also depends on label semantics.

examples.headline: Many eventual function-vector heads first show induction scores, which decline as function-vector scores rise.
Attention sinks form later than induction, with transition sharpness varying across model families.
Symbolic labels separate abrupt first-token translation gains from gradual second-token gains; semantic labels erase this.

related_findings.title: Toy learning transitions depend on the setup
related_findings.summary: In-context learning in toy settings can emerge abruptly, in stages or smoothly. Attention parametrisation, initialisation, task complexity and data size affect both the transition shape and whether learning succeeds.

examples.headline: Attention parametrisation changes regression learning from one abrupt drop to several staged drops.
Softmax attention jumps directly to copying, while linear attention first learns uniform pooling.
Increasing regression dimension turns reliable in-context learning into seed-dependent jumps and eventual failure.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Previous-token heads support several computations
related_findings.summary: Previous-token attention emerges in a similar training window across tested Pythia models, although its timing and layer placement vary. These heads also support computations beyond induction.

examples.headline: Previous-token attention emerges earlier and more strongly in larger Pythia models, with varying layer placement.
Previous-token heads appear in GPT2-Small indirect object identification routes, ranking highly in Llama 2-7B layers.
Previous-token-head ablation disrupts graph geometry represented from context; induction-head ablation preserves it.

related_findings.title: Induction over relations, functions and categories
related_findings.summary: Pretrained models show induction-like matching over semantic relations, functions and categories. Interventions link some of these patterns to task performance beyond exact token copying.

examples.headline: Previous-token heads feed function-induction heads whose ablation destroys Gemma-2 9B off-by-one addition contrast accuracy.
Multiple InternLM2-1.8B heads represent semantic relations more strongly than baselines using unrelated target entities.
Llama-3-8B heads match word categories, and blocking that pattern harms few-shot accuracy.

related_findings.title: Data and architecture shape small-model in-context learning
related_findings.summary: Depth, architecture and training-data structure affect whether small models improve with context. Task hierarchy and clustering of related examples (burstiness) also change the model scale or training needed for in-context learning.

examples.headline: Loss improvement with context depends on model depth, training progress and synthetic data entropy (randomness).
Deeper task hierarchies need larger models for in-context learning; errors fall more slowly with scale.
No evaluated architecture learns Omniglot in-context learning from purely non-bursty training; emergence timing varies.

related_findings.title: Mechanisms beyond copying
related_findings.summary: Abstractive recall and graph inference involve feed-forward networks or internal representations beyond direct copying. Dialogue demonstrations can also remain useful after their sequential structure is disrupted.

examples.headline: Removing upper feed-forward sublayers harms abstractive one-shot accuracy more sharply than extractive accuracy.
Swapping late-layer activations at the last token recovers most of Llama-3.1-8B's contrast between graph families.
Dialogue demonstrations retain benefits over context alone after both turns and tokens are shuffled.

related_findings.title: Copying depends on content and direction
related_findings.summary: Copying accuracy falls with a token-rarity proxy, while induction-head attribution drops for sufficiently altered repeats. Backward-copy attention remains weak even under explicit backward-copy training.

examples.headline: Random-token copying accuracy falls with tokenizer index, a proxy for token rarity.
Backward-copy attention remains near zero even with explicit backward-copy training.
Induction attribution drops sharply beyond substitution thresholds that increase with repeat length.

related_findings.title: Induction scores can miss relevant heads
related_findings.summary: Prefix-matching scores do not consistently identify selective or causally relevant heads. Their usefulness varies across model families and attention architectures.

examples.headline: Some GPT-2 heads retain strong key selectivity despite near-zero prefix-matching scores.
Induction scores identify arithmetic copying heads above chance in Gemma and Llama, but not Qwen.
Tests for striped attention patterns miss previous-token heads in some models; disabling them reveals their role.

related_findings.title: Task diversity and distribution shift constrain generalisation
related_findings.summary: Task diversity changes the regression estimator learned in context. Polynomial in-context learning degrades under coefficient shifts, while cipher accuracy differs across shifts.

examples.headline: Greater pretraining task diversity shifts regression predictions from discrete-prior optimal prediction (dMMSE) toward Ridge regression.
Polynomial in-context learning achieves near-zero in-distribution error but degrades sharply under coefficient shifts.
Qwen3-4B decodes shift-13 Caesar ciphers more accurately than shift-4 ciphers.

related_findings.title: Upstream circuits support induction in full transformers
related_findings.summary: Induction in pretrained full transformers depends on earlier computations involving previous tokens and duplicate tokens. Damage from ablating random heads can obscure which head sets matter, and tests for selectivity can miss necessary heads.

examples.headline: Previous-token head ablation nearly eliminates induction accuracy; random-head ablation also hurts, weakening attribution, especially in OLMoE.
Removing induction or previous-token paths sharply reduces GPT2-small agreement with original induction outputs.
OLMoE induction needs duplicate-token heads, including one never identified as induction-selective.

related_findings.title: Architectural shortcuts to induction
related_findings.summary: Shifting or mixing adjacent keys and values can enable induction in one layer or accelerate learning. Other architectural changes preserve copying while changing which projections carry it.

examples.headline: Convolving keys or values lets one-layer attention solve multi-query associative recall; query-only convolution fails.
One-layer attention shifting keys and values represents induction exactly, learning faster than two-layer standard attention.
Without value/output projections, the loss bump accompanying induction persists, copying improves and attention keys matter more.

related_findings.title: Loss transitions do not uniquely identify induction
related_findings.summary: Loss bumps and plateaus followed by drops also occur without attention-based induction heads. A change in training loss alone shows neither that a circuit formed nor that copying succeeded.

examples.headline: One-layer attention shows a loss bump despite flat multi-query associative recall accuracy; Mamba does too.
Recurrent neural networks show training-loss transitions on toy data despite lacking attention-based induction heads.
An N-gram-trained model shows loss plateaus and drops without developing induction heads.

related_findings.title: Copying across modalities and prediction schemes
related_findings.summary: Repeat-sensitive copying appears in biological sequence models, time-series models and diffusion language models. Its strength and responsible heads depend on architecture and available context.

examples.headline: Repeated protein and RNA sequences sharply reduce uncertainty, with effects varying across architectures.
A few sharp Chronos heads sustain forecast structure, though few meet standard induction criteria.
The diffusion language model's induction advantage depends on seeing both sides of the mask.

related_findings.title: Simple statistical solutions can precede contextual learning
related_findings.summary: Models can first learn individual-token frequencies (unigrams) or corpus-wide frequencies of token pairs (global bigrams) before acquiring richer mechanisms that use context. Some configurations remain at these simpler solutions.

examples.headline: Multilayer models trained on first-order Markov data plateau at unigram loss before reaching bigram solutions.
Global bigram statistics are learned faster than the in-context induction mechanism during joint training.
Pythia 12B improves loss with context earlier on unigrams than maximum-entropy (maximally unpredictable) bigram sequences.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Induction patterns can survive further training
related_findings.summary: Instruction tuning and continued training often preserve head-level induction or retrieval patterns. Multimodal and task-specific training can strengthen induction alongside in-context learning performance.

examples.headline: Base and instruction-tuned models retain highly correlated per-head induction scores.
Retrieval-head patterns persist across model variants but differ substantially between families.
Multimodal training and Qwen fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation strengthen induction; previous-token strength stays flat.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Copy heads influence repetition and prompt echo
related_findings.summary: Copy-related heads contribute to prompt echo and degenerate repetition in instruction-tuned models. Removing these heads can have the opposite effect on local repetition in GPT-2 small.

examples.headline: Disabling heads with high prefix-matching scores nearly eliminates prompt echo in small instruction-tuned models.
Copying heads gain causal influence during repetition; scaling them down improves following requested repetition lengths.
Induction-head ablation increases GPT-2 small’s nearby-text repetition; restoring head activity largely reverses this.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Retrieval heads support context-dependent answers
related_findings.summary: Small sets of retrieval or induction-like heads causally support long-context retrieval, many-shot classification and verbatim recall. Comparisons with interventions on random heads show that the importance of targeting these particular heads varies by task.

examples.headline: Masking sparse retrieval heads harms retrieval and extractive question answering more than masking random heads.
Masking top retrieval heads nearly eliminates in-context learning accuracy on Banking77-en-ICL in a model resembling LLaMA2.
Induction-head ablation collapses in-order list recall in Qwen and substantially reduces it in Llama-I.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Induction heads can persist after in-context learning fades
related_findings.summary: In-context learning can fade while training loss continues to improve and induction heads persist. Changes in earlier computations and competition with overall statistics learned in the weights can change what these heads do.

examples.headline: In-context learning can fade after emerging despite falling training loss, suggesting competition with weight-based learning.
Induction heads persist after in-context learning fades; altered earlier attention enables a strategy without such learning.
Next-token predictions balance pattern frequencies in context against pretrained statistics of consecutive token pairs.

related_findings.title: Repeated-list retrieval resembles short-term memory
related_findings.summary: Pretrained models retrieve repeated lists in an order-sensitive way that varies with training corpus, depth and position. These behavioural similarities do not by themselves establish an induction-head mechanism.

examples.headline: GPT-2 repeated-list retrieval depends strongly on training corpus and depth, with sensitivity to order.
Later list positions show stronger retrieval, while copying trajectories correlate with benchmark trajectories.
A contextual-memory model (CMR) fits top induction heads better than a Gaussian bell-curve baseline.

related_findings.title: Training data shapes copying
related_findings.summary: Repeated-data training can impair copying, and copying remains weak in a child-scale training setting. Evaluations across repetition levels must distinguish test-distribution changes from changes to training.

examples.headline: Training on repeated data sharply reduces copying recurring names in a one-layer attention-only model.
An attention-and-convolution model trained on BabyLM’s small corpus copies a repeated second half only weakly.
Copying tests measure generalisation across repetition levels after training at a single repetition setting.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: MLP neurons read induction-head outputs
related_findings.summary: Induction heads feed downstream neurons associated with confidence and repetition. Head ablations reduce these neurons' activity, while repetition-neuron ablations impair recall.

examples.headline: Joint induction-head ablation lowers GPT-2 Small entropy-neuron activity toward its level when text first appears.
Ablating late repetition neurons harms recall; ablating induction heads lowers those neurons’ activity.
Induction-head ablation reduces entropy-neuron magnitudes during decoding with retrieved information more than random-head ablation.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Induction-like patterns with frozen or random weights
related_findings.summary: Transformers with frozen random weights can develop induction-like attention after training their embeddings (the vectors representing input tokens), and previous-token signals can help random models match a current token sequence to earlier occurrences. Attention that ignores the input still performs poorly on tasks that require induction.

examples.headline: Training only token embeddings produces induction-like attention patterns in a two-layer transformer with frozen random weights.
Previous-token output patching raises random-model prefix matching; many top HAPAX heads suppress copied tokens.
Random attention ignoring inputs sharply harms induction-dependent tasks while preserving performance on algorithmic tasks and memorisation.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Induction interventions change how loss improves across context positions
related_findings.summary: Suppressing or ablating induction-like heads can make loss fall less from earlier to later context positions. Stronger signs of induction-like behaviour do not necessarily mean greater causal dependence on these heads.

examples.headline: Penalising attention to tokens following earlier matches lowers the in-context learning score in two-layer GPT2.
Synthetic-copy training strengthens signs of induction but makes ablation less damaging than using natural data alone.
Ablating CMR-like heads weakens loss reductions across context more than random ablation in most tested models.

related_findings.relationship_note: Related findings do not necessarily test an existing claim as worded.

related_findings.title: Multimodal in-context learning depends on image–text connections and labels
related_findings.summary: Demonstration images can contribute little compared with the query image and textual information. Learning arbitrary label mappings varies across vision-language models and can improve by adapting the early layers that combine image and text.

examples.headline: Removing demonstration images barely affects multimodal in-context learning; removing the query image causes large losses.
Adapting early layers joining image and text restores arbitrary-label learning where a late-layer adapter fails.
Zeroing either of two components (M1, M2) reduces in-context learning; zeroing M1 hurts more.

reading_list.why: Establishes the original induction-head account, its training transition, small-model causal evidence and limits at larger scales.
Separates contributions from induction heads and function vectors (task representations); conclusions depend on in-context learning measures and head selection.
Reports strong classification effects from disabling induction heads; random controls leave uncertainty about whether these effects are specific to induction.

known_gaps.summary: Uncertainty remains about whether effects are specific to induction heads, how results depend on the measure used, how independent replications are, how training data matters and whether circuit formation has distinct stages.
items: Studies disagree on whether Pythia-160M shows functioning induction behavior. The study reporting its absence lacks random controls matched to the induction-head intervention, uncertainty estimates and a stated model checkpoint (training snapshot).

Disabling randomly selected attention heads can also cause large classification losses, so it remains unclear whether the effects are specific to disabling induction heads. Classification accuracy and changes in loss from earlier to later tokens measure different aspects of performance and need separate interpretations.

Evidence that loss still improves on samples whose answers cannot be copied from context when induction behavior is suppressed rests on a main comparison with one random seed per condition. Numerical values in the relevant figures have not all been fully verified.

Apparent replication across papers may involve overlapping author groups, models or training runs. Independent support for how heads combine into circuits and for patterns in how they form during training remains unclear.

It remains unclear how the choice of tokenizer, which splits text into tokens, affects induction heads. Existing comparisons between training corpora still leave a need for controlled comparisons with matched evaluation conditions.

Circuit formation within the same training window can still proceed through ordered stages. Existing interpretations do not consistently distinguish events that share a training window from events that form a single transition.
